Reading an annual fee schedule: progressive slices, whole-balance bands and minimum charges

Four interactive charts show how the same listed rates can produce different annual invoices, how minimum and fixed fees enter the calculation, and what happens at a fee threshold.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read a hypothetical annual fee schedule in slices and whole-balance bands

Interactive planning lab

Progressive slices · total annual charge$1,670
Whole-balance band · total annual charge$1,370
Progressive total / selected fee base0.67%

Two invented annual fee formulas use the same rates, fixed thresholds, minimum asset charge and fixed annual account fee. Neither is a provider quote, a typical-market estimate or a recommended fee. The fee base is constant for this one-year quote; no average-balance, quarterly, prorated or market-value billing convention is inferred. Progressive charges apply each rate only to its slice. Whole-balance charges apply one rate to the entire fee base: up to and including CAD 100,000 uses the first rate; above CAD 100,000 through CAD 500,000 inclusive uses the middle rate; above CAD 500,000 uses the top rate. The minimum is applied to the asset charge FIRST, and the fixed annual fee is added once afterward. The hypothetical account remains open and both minimum and fixed fee can apply even at a zero base; no zero-balance waiver is assumed. Fees are a quote payable from outside the modeled asset base. No account deduction, investment path, return, tax deduction, sales tax, fund expense, transaction cost or service-quality adjustment is calculated. Rates may be edited in any order; statements about lower higher-band rates refer to the default schedule.

The central idea

A rate table needs a calculation rule. Establish which assets each rate applies to, where the minimum enters and which other charges remain before comparing annual dollars.

01

Start with the formula behind the rate table

A schedule that lists 0.8%, 0.5% and 0.3% does not give a complete invoice. It must also explain which assets receive each rate. Two schedules can display the same percentages while assigning them to different amounts.

This guide compares two deliberately specified formulas. Progressive pricing charges the first CAD 100,000 at the first rate, the next CAD 400,000 at the middle rate and any excess over CAD 500,000 at the top rate. Whole-balance pricing chooses a band from the total asset base and applies that band's single rate to every dollar.

The distinction is arithmetic. It does not establish which formula a particular provider uses or which service is preferable. The word “tiered” by itself is insufficient to resolve the calculation.

Investor.gov emphasizes the role of the advisory agreement in identifying services and charges. Its fee-disclosure explanation also distinguishes the advisory charge from other expenses that can apply. Those sources support asking for a complete formula; the numbers and schedules below are independently authored illustrations.

02

Cap each progressive slice before multiplying

At the default CAD 250,000 fee base, the first slice contains CAD 100,000 and the second contains CAD 150,000. There is no third-slice amount. The annual asset charge is CAD 100,000 × 0.8% plus CAD 150,000 × 0.5%, or CAD 1,550.

The middle rate applies only to the amount in its slice. Multiplying the entire CAD 250,000 by 0.5% gives a different formula. Likewise, charging the full CAD 400,000 middle slice when the client has only CAD 150,000 in it would bill assets that are absent from the stated base.

The waterfall exposes each component before the total. Empty slices remain zero, so the reader can see that crossing the first threshold does not erase the first slice or create an immediate full-sized second slice.

For nonnegative rates, this progressive asset charge is continuous at both thresholds. Its slope can change when the rate on the next dollar changes. That distinction between a change in slope and a jump in the bill matters when checking a quote near a boundary.

03

A whole-balance band reprices all of the stated base

The alternative formula places CAD 250,000 in the middle band and charges 0.5% on all CAD 250,000. Its asset charge is CAD 1,250. This is a valid description of the invented whole-balance formula, rather than the progressive calculation made incorrectly.

The boundaries are explicit: a balance of exactly CAD 100,000 remains in the first band; a balance above that amount and up to CAD 500,000 inclusive uses the middle band. Only an amount above CAD 500,000 uses the top band.

With descending rates, crossing a boundary can lower the total annual asset charge because the new rate applies to the entire base. The threshold chart compares exactly CAD 100,000 with CAD 100,100 and exactly CAD 500,000 with CAD 500,100. It does not connect widely spaced quotes with a smooth line that conceals repricing.

At the first default boundary, the progressive annual charge rises by CAD 0.50, while the whole-balance charge falls by CAD 299.50. At the second, the progressive charge rises by CAD 0.30 and the whole-balance charge falls by CAD 999.70. These are conditional differences in the selected formulas, not promised savings from adding assets to a real account.

04

Place the minimum and the fixed fee in the stated order

The example applies a CAD 300 minimum to the annual asset charge first. It then adds a separate CAD 120 annual account fee. The resulting formula is max(calculated asset charge, minimum asset charge) + fixed account fee.

At the default base, both calculated asset charges already exceed the minimum. The total quotes are therefore CAD 1,670 for progressive slices and CAD 1,370 for the whole-balance band. The CAD 300 difference comes from allocating the first slice to a different rate; the same CAD 120 fixed fee appears on both sides.

At a small enough balance, the minimum can set both quotes to the same amount. A minimum is a floor, not an extra CAD 300 added to every calculated charge. The waterfall's uplift row is only the positive amount required to reach that floor.

Other contracts may define a minimum on the final invoice, waive a fixed fee, combine accounts or suspend billing at zero assets. Those are different terms. This illustration keeps a hypothetical account open, with no zero-balance waiver, so a minimum and fixed fee can still produce a positive quote at a zero base.

05

Keep the total charge ratio separate from the next-dollar rate

The effective charge ratio divides the complete annual quote by the same stated fee base. For the default progressive example, CAD 1,670 ÷ CAD 250,000 is 0.668%, displayed as 0.67%. It includes the fixed fee and any minimum adjustment.

This ratio is not the rate charged on an additional dollar. In the middle progressive slice, a small additional amount receives the entered middle rate while earlier slice charges remain in place. An active minimum can temporarily prevent the invoice from increasing at all.

A zero fee base creates an undefined ratio even if the contract produces a positive charge. The headline therefore shows N/A at zero rather than displaying 0% or treating the ratio as an infinite investment loss.

The matrix uses positive balances to show how fixed and minimum charges affect the denominator. It is a fee-to-base comparison, not a fund expense ratio, an annual investment return or a judgment about service quality. Changing rates can also reverse the default ranking; neither formula is assumed always cheaper.

06

Reconcile an actual quote with its own billing terms

Before applying a real schedule, identify the assets included in the chargeable base. Ask whether the value is measured at a specific date or averaged over a period, how linked accounts are treated and whether cash or particular holdings receive different treatment.

Then establish the slice or band formula, exact threshold boundaries, the location of any minimum and the fixed charges included or excluded. Billing frequency, partial-year treatment and applicable taxes need their own terms. Dividing this annual illustration into four parts does not establish a provider's quarterly invoice.

The charts hold the base constant and treat the quoted fee as payable from outside it. They calculate no fee deduction from an account, return drag or future portfolio value. A model of ongoing deductions would need to specify when fees leave the account and how subsequent asset values affect later bills.

NASAA's fee-disclosure discussion highlights a formula clients can use to verify charges and agreement terms that match billing. The practical check is an itemized dollar calculation for the relevant base and period, followed by a separate comparison of the services received. A lower rate or invoice alone does not show that two engagements meet the same needs.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All rates, thresholds, balances and fees are invented examples. The charts compare one-year quotes at constant fee bases. They are not provider prices, investment projections or assessments of the value of advice. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
